Beállítom Románia megsemmisített két vízben sodródó, pilóta nélküli repülő szerkezetet a Fekete-tenger – közölte kedden Radu Miruta ügyvivő védelmi miniszter. A bejelentés szerint két orosz gyártmányú, Gerbera típusú, vélhetően robbanószerkezettel ellátott harci drónról és néhány dróndarabról volt szó, amelyeket a Neptun Deep gázmező közelében dolgozó civil hajósok vettek észre. Miután Ukrajna jelezte, hogy a drónok nem hozzájuk tartoznak, a parti őrség hajóján helyszínre küldött katonai búvárok felrobbantották azokat – írta az MTI. A vízben sodródó drónokat a hajózás biztonsága miatt semmisítették meg. A felrobbantott drónok néhány veszélytelen darabját kiemelte a parti őrség hajója – számolt be róla a Digi24 hírportál. A Gerbera típusú többcélú repülő szerkezeteket Oroszország fejlesztette ki az iráni Sahíd-136-oson alapuló Gerany-2-es drónok olcsóbb változataként. A Gerbera típusú drónokat főleg „csaliként” használják, hogy Ukrajna ezek semlegesítésére pazarolja el drága légelhárító rakétáit. A Gerbera-drónokat a légelhárító ütegek helyzetének beazonosítására, illetve jelerősítőként is használhatják más drónok távirányítása érdekében, ugyanakkor kis mennyiségű (6-8 kilogrammnyi) robbanóanyag szállítására is alkalmasak. A román kizárólagos gazdasági övezet keleti szélén, a nyílt vizek szomszédságában található Neptun Deep Románia legjelentősebb offshore gázlelőhelye, ahonnan becslések szerint mintegy 100 milliárd köbméternyi gáz termelhető ki. Az energiahordozó hasznosításának megkezdése 2027-re várható. Múlt hónapban Románia az orosz–ukrán háború kezdete óta először lelőtt egy, az ország légterébe hatoló orosz drónt. A beavatkozást követő napokon újabb rakétákkal válaszoltak az ismétlődő határsértésekre , a katonai válaszlépést pedig határozott diplomáciai lépések követték. Román elemzők szerint Oroszország a sorozatos légtérsértésekkel teszteli Románia új, aktívabb védelmi stratégiáját , valamint a NATO reakcióképességét. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz are visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran. Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/Reuters View image in fullscreen Vessels in the strait of Hormuz are visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran. Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/Reuters Iran Analysis Iran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodes Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Internal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterway Wed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Is the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme leader as “the pillar of Iran’s new security order”, and as transformative as possessing a nuclear weapon, in reality becoming a fast-diminishing asset, leaving Iran increasingly vulnerable to the new planned US wave of economic sanctions? It is the key debate that is raging inside Iran, with many different conclusions being drawn for Tehran’s negotiating strategy. Those who warn the strait’s value as a chokehold on the world economy will erode, leaving the country without foreign exchange reserves, argue that Iran’s negotiators should seek a deal soon. One analysis written by Hamid Paktinat, the founder of the Forum of Economic Activists, suggests the construction of alternative pipelines and export routes by Iran’s Gulf neighbours will halve the strait’s strategic value within three years. Those who worry about wasting assets inevitably set store by the separate visits this week to Tehran of Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, and Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir. These two men are critical to renegotiating the terms for the reopening of the strait and the revival of the discarded memorandum of understanding agreed by the US and Iran in June. ‘Economic D-day’: how desperate is Trump to end Iran war? — The Latest Read more The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have both recently made unusually blunt comments about the need to end the war – and the economic consequence of continuing it. Ghalibaf said that regardless of how much military power Iran possessed, “if people are hungry” and there was no economic growth, the country could not endure. Security, he argued, could not be sustained without a functioning economy. He added that, as someone with a military background, “we know the value of peace better than those who talk about peace”. Pezeshkian was even more blunt: “The war must end at some point,” he said. His argument was that Iran should end the conflict now, while Tehran still believes it is negotiating from a position of strength, rather than wait until its position weakens. The Iranian central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, also recently went on TV to warn about the economic pressures. “We are facing four or five major challenges simultaneously, including maximum sanctions, blockade, cutting off oil exports, and a budget imbalance, each of which puts pressure on the economy,” he said. “One of the neighbouring countries told me that if one-fifth of what happened in your country happened in our country, we would not be able to govern the country.” What is driving these remarks is the pressure on ordinary people in Iran, and an acceptance that the strait cannot become a permanent security doctrine in itself. Hamid Asefi, a Tehran-based journalist specialising in geo-economics, is one of many warning that if Hormuz is to be played as Iran’s final card every time a crisis arises, this card will gradually lose its value. “A threat that is constantly repeated turns from ‘deterrence’ into a political habit; and a political habit, if not accompanied by concrete achievements, sooner or later leads to an inflation of threats,” he said. The main question is no longer: can Iran close the strait, he wrote, but if Iran closes Hormuz to the world, does it open the door to power for itself or lock part of its power behind that door? “This is the Hormuz paradox. In international politics, a lever that is constantly flaunted can become its own enemy because it forces others to plan to reduce their vulnerability […] the main question of Iranian policy in Hormuz must change from: ‘How can we make the passage difficult?’ to ‘How can we make the passage so safe and stable that everyone needs Iran to maintain this order?’” That does not imply the lever is valueless. Far from it. Graph showing daily transits through strait of Hormuz According to data compiled by the ship tracker Kpler, only 112 oil and gas tankers went through the strait between 1 and 19 August. Almost 79% used unconfirmed routes, 19% used Iran’s preferred northern route and 2% used the Omani route. In reality many of the ships that used the unknown routes probably turned off their transponders and used US protection along the Oman route. It also appears that aided by the US government, Saudi, Emirati, Qatari and Kuwaiti oil companies have chartered a small group of oil tankers to take cargo through the southern route to the Gulf of Oman, where they then offload the oil to waiting tankers owned by their customers. Much of the risk is therefore transferred from shipping companies and oil customers to the more highly motivated state oil producers and to the US government. Iran has drawn up a blacklist of about 48 ships that it will try to ban or fine. But the US government is probably exaggerating the impact of these workarounds. Chris Wright, the US secretary of energy, claimed on 18 August the US navy had assisted in the transfer of more than 15m barrels of oil and other products. He also claimed the average daily transfer of oil through the strait was now more than 8m barrels, but even this figure is less than half the prewar average and is anyway seen as inflated. Most ship data trackers estimate the daily figure at closer to 6m barrels a day. Arsenio Dominguez, the secretary general of the International Maritime Organization, furthermore dismissed Donald Trump’s outlandish claim that the US navy had all but opened the strait, telling Bloomberg: “Given the very small number of ships that transit the strait of Hormuz, it is clear that this strait is, in practice, not open.” The US president has countered that all mines in the strait have been removed, leaving Iranian drone and naval attacks as the chief threat. But the fact that before the war the strait accounted for 20% of oil and oil-related products is serving as a catalyst for the restructuring of the global energy infrastructure. Countries in the Gulf are rapidly building a network of alternative pipelines, with the aim of protecting more than half of their prewar exports from the impact of Hormuz by the end of this decade. Paktinat has looked through the region at the capacity, length and cost of pipelines being prepared in six countries over the next one to four years. He concluded Saudi Arabia’s reliance on the strait of Hormuz would decrease from 70% to 15%. The UAE’s reliance would decrease from 50% to 15%, and Iraq’s dependence would fall from 100% to 30%. Kuwait and Qatar’s reliance would decrease from 100% to less than half. Bahrain’s reliance would fall from 100% to 15%, he assessed. Finally, Oman’s reliance would change from 0% to becoming a major coastal oil transfer hub for the entire region. Overall, he says, the strategic value of the strait of Hormuz will be halved within three years and almost lost within six years with the implementation of these projects. The narrow horseshoe waterway will remain, but its strategic importance – the centre of Iranian gravity – will have evaporated. In the meantime, the US will try to turn Trump’s premature boast that the Iranian economy has completely collapsed into reality. It will try once again to block the vital arteries of the Iranian government across five key sectors: gold, cryptocurrency, technology, shipping and aviation. Success is by no means guaranteed, as Trump must know from the failure to defeat Iran in his first term. But slowly chipping away at Iran’s economic resilience until the strait finally becomes an irrelevance may be Trump’s only remaining option. Beállítom A Szabályozott Tevékenységek Felügyeleti Hatósága (SZTFH) a következetes hatósági fellépés és a kiszámítható szabályozási környezet letéteményese. A hatóság kedden kiadott közleményével arra reagált, hogy a megszüntetésének lehetőségét vizsgálja a kormány. A hétfői Magyar Közlönyben jelent meg, hogy Magyar Péter miniszterelnök határozatban hívta fel Görög Márta igazságügyi minisztert: készítsen jelentést arról, hogy tudná a kormány megszüntetni a Szabályozott Tevékenységek Felügyeleti Hatóságát (SZTFH). A hatóság az MTI-hez is eljuttatott közleményében azt írta, hogy a felügyelete alá tartozó ágazatok gazdasági potenciálja nemzetgazdasági szinten is meghatározó: az érintett, jellemzően magyar tulajdonú kis- és középvállalkozások éves szinten több 10 ezer milliárd forintos árbevételt realizálnak, és több mint 50 ezer magyar állampolgár számára biztosítanak közvetlenül munkalehetőséget. Közleményük szerint a felügyelt tevékenységek stabil működése a központi költségvetés szempontjából is jelentős: az érintett gazdasági szektorokból származó állami adó- és járulékbevételek éves szinten meghaladják az 1000 milliárd forintot, ami alapvető fontosságú a közszolgáltatások fenntartásában – tették hozzá. A SZTFH szerint a különböző szakterületeken egyaránt nemzetközi mércével is kiemelkedő szaktudással rendelkező, összességében több mint 400 munkatársának köszönhetően az SZTFH mára az államigazgatási szervezetrendszerbe jól beilleszkedett, a nemzetközi hatósági együttműködés rendszerében is ismert és elismert, gyorsreagálású hatóság, amely feladatait mindenkor magas színvonalon, átlátható és kiszámítható módon végzi. Kitértek arra is, hogy mindenben együttműködnek a kormányhatározatban kijelölt miniszterrel a jogi átvilágítás hatékony teljesítése érdekében. A Szabályozott Tevékenységek Felügyeleti Hatóságát 2021-ben hozta létre az akkori Orbán-kormány, a hatóság azóta egymástól teljesen független, semmilyen módon nem összefüggő területeket felügyel. Ezek között van többek között a dohánykereskedelem, a bányászat, a szerencsejáték és a végrehajtás, a bányászati tevékenységek, a kőolaj-, földgáz- és geotermikus energia-kitermelés biztonsági és hatósági felügyelete is. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj20.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The ICC said it would not be "deterred" by the sanctions By Tom Bateman ,Â State department correspondent ,Â Anna Holligan ,Â Reporting from in The Hague, Â and Â Florence Freeman Published 9 October 2026 The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Marco Rubio said that "either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC" The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday. "Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz said. Merz said Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses. Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies. Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez https://p.dw.com/p/5PmP2 Skip next section DW in Berlin: Could Ukraine NATO membership become reality? 11/23/2026 November 23, 2026 DW in Berlin: Could Ukraine NATO membership become reality? Maximiliane Koschyk in Berlin For delegates at the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin on Monday, the question of Ukrainian membership of NATO wasn't new. "It is a tragedy that, in 2008, Ukraine asked to become a member of NATO and who said no? France and Germany ," said Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, a German member of the European Parliament. "I think we have to fix it." Yet not all German delegates agree: "To become a member is a difficult question because it can also increase tensions," said Roman Poseck, interior mnister of the German state of Hesse. "Therefore, Germany in particular is not really in favor of this at the moment." When pressed by delegates in a plenary debate, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul kept it vague, saying: "Ukraine is on an irreversible path towards NATO. I would say this is our position and let's see how and if it will work specifically." Other delegates were careful not to preempt any official processes. "We have to make these decisions based on facts, based on [Ukraine's] readiness to become a member and, of course, after discussions with our own countries," cautioned Canadian delegate Cheryl Gallant. "I think the most important thing for Ukraine, but also for all of the members of the alliance, is that there are durable security guarantees for the Ukrainian people," added Philipp Brickell, a delegate for the United Kingdom . After last week's Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin saw US Special Envoy Jared Kushner float the option of "Article Five-like" security guarantees, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday again pushed for the real deal (see below). "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" he said. "Why not say out loud what so many people think?" He received support in particular from Nordic allies who, with the Russian invasion of Ukraine now well into its fifth year, are keen to strengthen Europe and NATO and boost security on the alliance's northern flank. Ville Vayrynen, the Finnish President of the Nordic Council, said of Ukrainian NATO membership: "That's something that I would gladly welcome if that's the direction we're going to go, and I strongly support that idea." Edited by: Kieran Burke https://p.dw.com/p/5PlIp Skip next section Zelenskyy: 'NATO is the answer' 11/23/2026 November 23, 2026 Zelenskyy: 'NATO is the answer' Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday renewed his calls for full membership of NATO, arguing that Ukraine's hard-won combat experience, its cutting-edge defense industry and large military would be a benefit for the alliance. "NATO is the answer – and with a strong Ukrainian army, NATO itself is guaranteed to be stronger," Zelensky told the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video link. A number of NATO leaders have expressed hesitation about bringing Ukraine into the alliance, with United States envoy Jared Kushner saying last week that Washington might consider offering Kyiv a security guarantee similar to that provided under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty as part of a peace settlement. But Zelenskyy said major questions remain about how such guarantees would work without full NATO commitment. "Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again? What exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all this cost? And will it really work?" he asked. "All of this is not easy and so far we have not heard clear specific answers." Rutte: Not all NATO members in agreement NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte underscored the alliance's support for Ukraine but noted that membership would require unanimous support. "Not all NATO allies agree at this moment [on] letting Ukraine become a member," he said, while also firmly rejecting the idea that outside powers like Russia could dictate who joins the alliance. "Who becomes a member of NATO is decided by NATO alone," he said. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance." As for whether the prospect of Ukrainian membership of NATO could be part of talks with Russia, Rutte said: "In order to speculate about such talks, we would actually have to have the talks."
